newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Spain's jobless down, reform still vital.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Spain's jobless down, reform still vital.

text.p: Spain's unemployment continued its downward trend in the third quarter but the jobless rate remains the highest in Europe and Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar said far-reaching labour reforms were still vital.
Figures from the National Statistics Institute released on Tuesday showed unemployment fell to 3.51 million in the third quarter compared with 3.56 million in the same period of 1995.
This represents a jobless rate of 21.91 percent compared with 22.73 percent in the third quarter of 1995.
Despite the improvement, Aznar reaffirmed his commitment to labour reform and said the government would not shy away from carrying out as many structural changes as were necessary.

Analysts said the figures had surpassed expectations but agreed that labour reforms were still a necessity to free the economy of one of the most rigid labour structures in Europe and ensure a solid reduction in unemployment.
Shortly after taking office, Aznar said his priority was to reach a German-style jobs pact with unions to tackle Spain's towering unemployment.
But early talks failed and Aznar gave the unions and employers until Spring 1997 to come up with a preliminary agreement before the government would step in again.
The government has now tightened the deadline to the first weeks of 1997 and said it would back the introduction of a more flexible "hire and fire" policy in the labour market.
But analysts were sceptical that an agreement on the key issues would be reached by then.
They noted the commitment to reforms also come at a time when the government's relationship with unions and employers was far from easy, but Aznar still stepped up the pressure.

"An agreement where everything remains as is would not be sufficient. In a matter of such importance for the development of the country, the government...will act accordingly," Aznar said at a seminar on Tuesday.

Spain's principal trade unions have said they will call a nationwide strike on December 12 to protest a freeze on public-sector wages which the government enforced to help whip the country's finances into shape for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
The government earlier upset employers with a pensions deal which they denounced as over-generous and refused to sign.
But analysts said labour reform was vital if Spain was to be on an even par with other countries in EMU.
Spain continues to stress the importance of growth in easing unemployment but analysts said this was not enough.
"Spain needs serious reforms to ensure that growth is translated into employment growth," said one economist.
Analysts said, however, they were more encouraged than in previous quarters by Tuesday's unemployment data.
"The data reveal an important creation of jobs only surpassed at the beginning of 1990 when the economy was growing at around four percent," said Banco Central Hispano in a statement.
Analysts said the annual jobs growth rate was very encouraging at 3.2 percent, 0.6 percent above that in the previous quarter.

"Employment has increased significantly, especially in permanent jobs for males, breaking with the trend seen in previous quarters where job creation was largely in temporary contracts for females," Argentaria added.
